_readme: Reference numbers for the 'Mission environment' card: radiation baselines and one-way signal delay for each place a crew might be. Every radiation figure is quoted from the source named next to it. Delay values are CALCULATED (distance divided by the speed of light), not quoted; JPL Horizons gives exact values for any date if you want them later.

limits.label: Career effective-dose limit
limits.note: Universal for all ages and sexes.

limits.label: Single solar particle event design limit
limits.note: Effective dose per design reference event.

limits.label: Storm-shelter shielding
limits.note: Shielding cuts dose by about 50% on average for a solar particle event but only about 7% for galactic cosmic rays.

environments.label: Space station (low Earth orbit)
environments.doseNote: Add an ISS dose rate here once the team picks a NASA source for it.

environments.label: Moon (orbit, Gateway or surface base)
environments.doseNote: Add a lunar dose rate here once the team picks a NASA source for it (Artemis data is a candidate).
environments.delayNote: Calculated: average Earth-Moon distance 384,400 km divided by the speed of light.
environments.autonomy: A short back-and-forth with the ground is still possible.

environments.label: Deep-space transit to Mars
environments.doseNote: Measured by the Radiation Assessment Detector inside Curiosity on the 2011-2012 trip to Mars; about 3% came from solar particles. NASA's brief uses 1.5 mSv/day as a transit planning example.
environments.delayNote: Calculated from Earth-Mars distances of roughly 55 to 400 million km. Changes with the planets' positions.
environments.autonomy: A question and answer can take up to about 44 minutes, so the crew has to decide alone.

environments.label: Mars surface base
environments.doseNote: Surface-environment figure in NASA's radiation technical brief. Confirm in the brief that it refers to Mars before submission.
environments.autonomy: The crew has to decide alone for most events.
